en: This key makes it possible to formulate, in more rigorous terms, the idea of personal integrity in the consumption of IOCs. It is not exhausted in physical or psychological integrity in the classical sense, but reaches informational and biographical integrity, because the subject also comes to project themselves socially through their digital records, their accumulated trajectory and their recognizable position in the ecosystem. Data, records, profiles and histories are not only economically exploitable informational collections; they function as a direct representation of personality and, to a certain extent, as its extension in the digital environment <1>Doneda</1><2>(Doneda, 2020, p. 146-147; p. 149)</2><3><4>563</4></3>. In contemporary terms, this means recognizing that the so-called digital dossiers <5>p. 536</5> constitute a new type of identity and that personal data are connected to the free exercise and development of the human personality <6>Laprano</6><7>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141; p. 153)</7><8><9>564</9></8>. Consequently, erasures, blocks, resets and suppressions of trajectory cannot automatically be reduced to mere patrimonial loss.

This perception has an older dogmatic basis than is sometimes admitted. The legal protection of the person is not exhausted in protection against physical aggression or economic loss, reaching also intellectual, emotional and biographical life. The old formulation of Warren and Brandeis is useful here precisely because it shows that the law, over time, had to recognize that thoughts, emotions, sensations and other immaterial forms of existence also call for legal protection, not on the exclusive basis of property, but on the broader idea of inviolate personality <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 2-3; p. 10])</2><3><4>565</4></3>. This historical <5>p. 537</5> opening matters because it legitimizes the passage from the patrimonial to the existential without turning theoretical reflection into delirium. Thus, what is asserted is only that the integrity of the consumer may include the preservation of minimum conditions of biographical continuity and stability of symbolic insertion, and not only the refund of a frustrated purchase.

In continuous services, this takes on very concrete contours. The consumer's trajectory is not a mere passive “record” kept by the platform, nor an informational deposit without a subject. It is a biographical result produced by repeated choices, performance, investment of time, acquisition, cooperation, accumulation of signs of belonging and permanence in the ecosystem. Even though this construction takes place under the mediation of the <1>Lex Plataformae</1>, it remains attributable to the consumer as an expression of biographical continuity within the supply regime. For this reason, certain IOCs operate as trajectory assets and not merely as one-off utilities. What accumulates is a bundle of memory, identity and recognition, so that its unilateral suppression or reclassification cannot be treated as a simple irrelevant technical variation. Data protection, moreover, becomes insufficient when read in a purely patrimonial frame, because this subordinates the person to the market value of their own information and lowers the priority of the development of personality <2>Doneda</2><3>(Doneda, 2020, p. 145-146; p. 269; p. 288)</3><4><5>566</5></4>.

At this point, the value of the IOC must also be reconstructed as symbolic architecture. Certain objects and trajectory marks are worth less for what they “do” in utilitarian terms and more for what they mean in the ecosystem: status, rarity, belonging, memory of participation, distinction and social recognition. What is consumed, then, is not only functional performance, but also symbolic position. The civil protection of personality reaches precisely the way in which the person is projected, recognized and situated in the social milieu, <1>p. 538</1> which is why reputation, honor and identity receive protection not because they are simple intimate feelings, but because they make up objective relational dimensions of the person's life <2>Schreiber</2><3>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 71; p. 211)</3><4><5>567</5></4>. In digital ecosystems, the loss of an account, of history, of accumulated signs and of continuity of trajectory may, therefore, transcend economic utility and touch legally cognizable reputational and identity dimensions.

The formulation is reinforced when one observes that persistent records and social classifications can compress the singularity of the person and affect the way they are apprehended and positioned in the social world. The protection of identity does not protect only formal signs, but the faithful presentation of the person in their singularity, preventing compressions, falsifications and fixations produced by third parties <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 155-156; p. 216)</2><3><4>568</4></3>. On platforms, this means that the history of enjoyment, the signs of belonging and the accumulated marks of participation are not merely technical remnants of the experience; they take part in the way the consumer is recognized within the environment and, in certain cases, outside it. The IOC comes to operate as a biographical and identity asset.

Here too the informational background matters. Data, traces and monitoring concern the personal integrity of the user in a digital environment because they take part in the way their social and individual identity is projected, organized and exposed. Data protection must consider the physical and electronic body of the subject, and not only the abstract circulation of information <1>Costa</1><2>(Costa, 2018, p. 41; p. 44; p. 47)</2><3><4>569</4></3>. For this reason digital traces cannot be <5>p. 539</5> reduced to economically exploitable assets, since they interfere with social classification, autonomy and self-determination, and are more adequately understood as a dimension of personality itself <6>Costa</6><7>(Costa, 2018, p. 44; p. 47)</7><8><9>570</9></8>. The digital environment, in short, is not only a market; it is also a space of identity projection and of existential impact.

On the consumer-law plane, the argument must keep its feet on the ground. Contractual and consumer-law protection is not exhausted in the control of price or in the correction of narrow patrimonial imbalances. In relationships marked by vulnerability, dependence and continued trust, the rebalancing that can be required must extend to loyal and dignified treatment and protect legitimate expectations that go beyond the mere economic account <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 290; p. 1481)</2><3><4>571</4></3>. This is the limit that prevents the existential aspect from drifting away from consumer law. The CDC already offers sufficient grammar to recognize that the injury may reach quality of life, trust and the practical integrity of the consumption experience, and not only the consumer's pocket in the narrow sense.

This broadening of protection has direct repercussions on legal remedies. When the consumer relationship frustrates legitimate expectations as to the adequacy, utility, safety or <1>p. 540</1> quality of the performance, the consumer-law system is not automatically oriented toward the residual monetization of the loss. It seeks, in the first place, to materially restore the consumer's position, satisfy their interests and avoid greater harm, including in a non-patrimonial dimension <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 1383; p. 856)</3><4><5>572</5></4>. Hence the importance of Article 35 of the CDC<6><7>573</7></6>, which allows one to demand forced performance of the obligation, accept an equivalent performance or rescind the contract with losses and damages, and of Article 84<8><9>574</9></8>, which enshrines specific relief of the obligation and a practical result equivalent to performance. In long-lasting IOCs, these provisions support the primacy of functional restoration, and not the automatic conversion of every loss into money. First one tries to restore the position of enjoyment; only afterwards is an alternative for reparation considered.

This point is crucial in view of the platform's own contractual frame. Clause 2.3 of Riot's Terms of Service provides that, once the account is terminated, the user loses access to the account, to the associated data, to the in-game currency and to virtual content, without refund in cases of just cause, with the further possibility of cancellation of other accounts and of access to other services<1><2>575</2></1>. The clause is valuable because it lays the problem bare: what is lost is not only an isolated item, <3>p. 541</3> but the overall position of enjoyment, the history, the inventory, the trajectory and the practical continuity of insertion in the ecosystem. Exclusivity is exercised, here, as a power of complete erasure of the consumed experience, which prevents treating sanction, exclusion or rollback as mere internal adjustments without existential legal relevance.

It is precisely for this reason that the subsection works with the idea of a digital existential minimum. The expression does not serve to rhetorically inflate any online discomfort into the category of constitutional drama. Its function is more restrained: to designate a core of stability and continuity that can be required in long-lasting IOCs with a high identity load, such as account, history, progression, reputation and inventory, so as to prevent unilateral erasures and reconfigurations from being naturalized as “mere internal policy” immune to control. In qualified cases, the loss of an account, history or trajectory may constitute moral damages for injury to personality, especially when it affects in an objectifiable way biographical continuity, institutionalized belonging in the ecosystem or relevant anchors of reputation and memory, and not mere subjective annoyance. Here, moreover, the methodological parallel with aesthetic damage is useful: Brazilian law already knows movements of categorial refinement to prevent injuries to the person from being swallowed by overly generic headings, which legitimizes, by methodological analogy, greater analytical density for injuries to the digital trajectory and to biographical continuity <1>Lopez</1><2>(Lopez, 2021, p. 31-33; p. 78)</2><3><4>576</4></3>.

The institutional consequence of this reading falls on the platform's own governance. If it administers access, permanence, visibility, sanctions and paths of participation, then it also administers inclusion and exclusion in the digital social space. From this follows the need for minimum parameters of private due process: verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence, procedural predictability and intelligible avenues of challenge. This requirement does not derive from the company's benevolence, but from the public relevance of the effects produced by its governance on the memory, reputation, continuity of trajectory and symbolic <1>p. 542</1> position of the consumer. The administration of someone else's digital biography cannot operate as a sovereign black box.

At this point, the LGPD provides important reinforcements. The use of data linked to the consumer's trajectory, history and digital biography must remain compatible with the stated purposes and with the context of the relationship<1><2>577</2></1>, must be intelligible to the data subject<3><4>578</4></3>, and does not eliminate the rights to confirmation of existence, access, correction, deletion or portability of processed data<5><6>579</6></5>. It also presupposes secure management of relevant records and trails<7><8>580</8></7>. These provisions do not turn the consumer into the absolute owner of everything the platform records, but they reinforce that their digital biography is not raw mass entirely unavailable to the data subject and that the administration of the memory of enjoyment must remain controllable, intelligible and minimally accessible.

There is also a systemic parallel especially useful for preventing simplistic objections. The Copyright Law recognizes, in Article 24, item VII, the author's moral right to access a single and rare copy of the work that is legitimately in the possession of another in order to preserve its memory<1><2>581</2></1>. The point is not to turn the consumer into an author, nor to transplant the regime of authorial moral rights into the consumer-law field. The point is narrower and more elegant: the Brazilian legal order already admits, in another domain, that the preservation of memory linked to an immaterial object under the control of a third party may justify minimum positive duties of access and of enabling a record. This suffices to dismiss the superficial objection according to which the absence of full ownership would, by itself, eliminate any legal relevance of interests of memory, preservation and continuity.

This parallel even helps to prepare the fit with the discussion of Intellectual Property developed further on. If the platform depends on the continuous participation of the consumer to produce economic value and vitality of the ecosystem, then there is a core of trajectory and memory produced in the relationship that cannot be treated as disposable residue <1>p. 543</1> of supply. The consequence is not to make the consumer an author, but to recognize that erasures, resets, inventory exclusions, suppressions of history and sanctions that eliminate the biography built in the environment require verifiable reasoning, minimum preservation of records and, where appropriate, restoration through reinstatement of the position of enjoyment. What is lost, in these cases, is not only access, but biographical continuity objectified within the governed regime itself.

With this, the subsection fixes the reference legal interests that make the IOC legally visible beyond immediate exchange value. The protected core of enjoyment comes to include personal integrity and symbolic identity, objectified in history, reputation, memory, belonging and continuity of trajectory. The signs of relevant degradation also become clearer: reputational exclusion, loss of functional equivalence, access restrictions, erasure of history and unilateral mutability of structuring elements of the consumer's position. Protection ceases to operate under an institutional blindness that converts every conflict into price and residual compensation and comes to admit, on the basis of the system itself, remedies of functional restoration, preservation of trails, access to records, procedural correction and restoration of the position of enjoyment whenever this is possible and legally due. This is the basis that will allow, further on, the formulation of open auditability, the distribution of burdens and finer standards of restoration in the regime of the IOC.

The dispute over losses, blocks or suppressions in digital environments need not remain imprisoned in the language of patrimonial loss or of simple non-performance, because contemporary civil protection already recognizes that certain injuries reach the person in an existentially relevant dimension, and not only the things he possesses. The rereading of private law in light of human dignity breaks precisely with the excessively patrimonialist perspective that confined the legal problem to the economic value of the affected good, requiring attention also to the existential projections of the person in the social world <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 10)</2>. When records, signs, usage trajectories, digital historicity and symbolic belongings come to structure objectifiable forms of personal continuity, the corresponding impairment no longer fits comfortably within the narrow grammar of the lost price. This key becomes even sharper when the injury is understood not from the suffering subjectively experienced, but from the attribute of personality objectively affected. The advantage of this formulation lies precisely in preventing the protection of the person from depending on sentimental proof or on dramatization of the harm, concentrating instead on the legally protected projection that was violated <3>Schreiber</3><4>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 17)</4>. This is precisely what matters here: in continuous digital ecosystems, there may be a legally cognizable impairment of dimensions of personality mediated by records, positions of enjoyment, objectified memory and signs of insertion in the environment. <5>↩</5>

The digital experience may reach legally relevant dimensions of personal integrity that go beyond strict patrimonial interests, because data protection, informational self-determination and the free development of personality make up the existential core of the person in an informational environment. Along these lines, the specific protection of personal data appears as a means of guaranteeing fundamental rights already enshrined, such as liberty and privacy, as well as others developed more recently, among them informational self-determination and the free development of personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 139)</2>. This articulation deepens when it is affirmed that informational self-determination is directed precisely at the free development of the personality of the data subject, which is why any interpretation that distorts it, for example through unrestricted consent harmful to that development, must be considered unacceptable <3>Laprano</3><4>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 148)</4>. In reinforcement, informational self-determination and the centrality of the data subject appear as means of enhancing the free determination and free development of the personality of the natural person, giving him instruments to control the processing of his data, including as to confirmation of the existence of processing, correction, modification and deletion <5>Laprano</5><6>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155-156)</6>. The integrity of the person, in digital environments, may thus involve not only patrimonial goods, but also informational integrity, biographical continuity and minimum conditions of personal self-determination. <7>↩</7>

Digital data, records, profiles and histories do not constitute only economically exploitable informational collections. By reason of the privileged bond between personal information and the subject to whom it refers, these elements function as a direct representation of his personality and, to that extent, as a true extension of it <1>Doneda</1><2>(Doneda, 2020, p. 146-147)</2>. When the digital environment operates on histories, traces, profiles and personal records, it is not merely manipulating neutral content or abstract utilities, but acting upon legally qualified projections of the person himself. This impact intensifies when the profile built from the data becomes the main visible aspect of the individual before third parties. In these cases, the electronic representation may function as a true virtual persona, merging, in certain circumstances, with the very person to whom it refers <3>Doneda</3><4>(Doneda, 2020, p. 149)</4>. The reference to the electronic body, to the <5>digital persona</5> or to the avatar expresses the mutation according to which the person comes to project himself in the digital environment through data, histories and records whose manipulation, blocking, distortion or suppression affects not only economic interests, but also identity, biographical continuity and personal position in the ecosystem <6>Doneda</6><7>(Doneda, 2020, p. 149)</7>. For this reason, in long-lasting immaterial objects of consumption, erasures, sanctions and losses of trajectory cannot automatically be reduced to mere patrimonial loss. <8>↩</8>

The digital environment cannot be read only as a space for the economic circulation of assets, contracts and data, because injuries that fall directly on the person in his existential dimension are also projected in it. The repersonalization of private law, in this context, places back at the center the tension between the demands of an impersonal, economically oriented market and the need to protect the fundamental rights of the natural person subjected to external influences <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141)</2>. This reading gains density when it is recognized that data processing activities have a growing interference in people's lives and that the so-called digital dossiers constitute a “new type of identity”, which is why the correction of this information becomes essential for the identity of the data subject to be projected faithfully, dogmatically justifying the inclusion of personal data in the category of personality rights <3>Laprano</3><4>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 153)</4>. In reinforcement, personal data are qualified as a “true extension of the free exercise and development of the human personality”, so that informational self-determination is not justified by mere ownership of data, but by its indissoluble relationship with the personality of the data subject <5>Laprano</5><6>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 153)</6>. Thus, in governed digital environments, the injury may fall not only on patrimony or immediate economic utility, but on informational integrity, identity projection, biographical continuity and the development of personality. <7>↩</7>

Here, Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis offer a classical foundation that is particularly useful for showing that the legal protection of the person is not exhausted by protection against physical aggression or patrimonial loss. In reconstructing the historical evolution of rights, the authors show that the law progressively came to recognize the spiritual, intellectual and sensitive dimension of human existence, extending the reach of legal protection beyond corporeal things. As they state, there was recognition of man's “spiritual nature”, of his “feelings and his intellect”, so that the right to life itself came to mean also “the right to enjoy life”, while property expanded to encompass “intangible, as well as tangible” forms of possession <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 2])</2>. This movement appears even more explicitly when they argue that the intensification of intellectual and emotional life made it evident that only part of the pain, pleasure and profit of life lies in physical things, which is why “thoughts, emotions, and sensations demanded legal recognition” <3>Brandeis</3><4>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 3])</4>. In addition, in examining the protection of personal writings and productions, they state that the corresponding protective principle rests not, properly speaking, on private property, but on an “inviolate personality” <5>Brandeis</5><6>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 10])</6>. The integrity of the consumer, in continuous digital ecosystems, may comprise the preservation of minimum conditions of biographical continuity, built trajectory, symbolic insertion and stability of enjoyment, without thereby dissolving the analysis into psychologism or depriving the CDC of its protective centrality. <7>↩</7>

The protection of personal data does not fit adequately within a purely patrimonial frame. Treating personal information as a simple economic good or as a circulable asset subject to a proprietary logic impoverishes protection precisely because it subordinates the person to the market value of his own data, when what is at stake is a much broader existential dimension <1>Doneda</1><2>(Doneda, 2020, p. 145-146)</2>. The insufficiency of this reading becomes clear once one observes that, in many contemporary social relationships, the individual is recognized only indirectly, through the representation of his personality that his personal data provide <3>Doneda</3><4>(Doneda, 2020, p. 269)</4>. The legal problem, therefore, is not only the economic use of information, but the projection of the person's identity through it. For this reason, a predominantly proprietary protection of personal data comes into tension with its qualification as a fundamental right, since it subjects the debate to paradigms that weaken the priority of the development of personality and reduce the person to the status of an object of informational circulation <5>Doneda</5><6>(Doneda, 2020, p. 288)</6>. As a consequence, histories, profiles, records and other digital traces must be protected not only because they have economic value or business utility, but because they make up the identity, biographical continuity and informational integrity of the subject in a digital environment. <7>↩</7>

The civil protection of personality reaches not only subjective interiorities, but also the way in which the person is projected, recognized and situated in the social milieu. Reputation and honor receive their own legal protection: not because they represent simple intimate feelings, but because they make up objective relational dimensions of the person's life, socially relevant and normatively protected <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 71)</2>. In digital environments, the loss of an account, of history, of accumulated signs, of relational position or of continuity of trajectory may, in certain cases, transcend the language of economic utility and touch legally cognizable dimensions of reputation and identity. This conclusion is reinforced when personal identity is treated not as merely formal data, but as protection of the right to be oneself in the social space, that is, of respect for the traits, experiences, convictions and marks that set the person apart before others <3>Schreiber</3><4>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 211)</4>. The point carries particular weight here because it allows us to understand that certain digitally mediated elements cease to be perceived only as isolated assets or functionalities and come to make up forms of the person's social presentation. <5>↩</5>

The persistence, organization and manipulation of socially relevant records may have direct repercussions on the dignity and existential integrity of the person, because informational standardization tends to reduce his singularity to profiles, classifications and framings built by third parties. When data and records come to be used to fix representations of the individual, there is a civilly relevant risk of compression of his singularity and of impairment of the way he will be apprehended, treated and positioned in the social world <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 155-156)</2>. The legal problem of digital records is not limited to their economic circulation, since it also involves the protection of the person against fixations, distortions or losses that affect his social presentation and his biographical continuity. This perception fits well with the dynamic dimension of personal identity. The protection of identity does not protect only formal signs, but the faithful presentation of the person in his singularity, preventing falsifications or undue compressions of the elements by which he is individualized in the social whole <3>Schreiber</3><4>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 216)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Data, traces and monitoring do not concern only the abstract circulation of information on the network, but the very personal integrity of the user in a digital environment. Data protection must consider the social and individual identity of the user, as well as his “physical and electronic body”, precisely so that adequate means of protection can be built <1>Costa</1><2>(Costa, 2018, p. 41)</2>. This formulation shifts the debate from the purely technical-informational plane to the plane of the person, showing that processed data and captured traces do not hover outside the subject, but take part in the way his identity is projected, organized and exposed in the digital environment. The same reading is reinforced when data protection appears as an expression of the very liberty and dignity of the person, so that data cannot serve the objectification of the individual nor his transformation into a target of constant surveillance <3>Costa</3><4>(Costa, 2018, p. 44)</4>. In addition, the creation of mechanisms of knowledge and control over personal data constitutes a direct expression of the protection of personality rights, since, when the object of the data is a subject of rights, the information must be understood as an attribute of personality <5>Costa</5><6>(Costa, 2018, p. 47)</6>. <7>↩</7>

Traces, monitoring and data processing legally affect the integrity of the person because they interfere with his social classification, his autonomy and his power of self-determination in a digital environment. The protection of personal data may be understood as a new personality right, and not as a simple offshoot of a supposed patrimonial dominion of the individual over his data, which is why it proves inadequate to treat the person as a mere owner of information about himself <1>Costa</1><2>(Costa, 2018, p. 44)</2>. The consequence is direct: digital traces cannot be reduced to economically exploitable informational assets, since they bear on existential projections of the person himself. This reading is reinforced when the recognition of the protection of personal data as an autonomous and fundamental right appears linked precisely to the risks that automated processing imposes on personality rights, being grounded in substantive equality, liberty, the dignity of the human person and privacy <3>Costa</3><4>(Costa, 2018, p. 47)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Consumer-law protection is not exhausted by the control of price nor by the restoration of strict patrimonial imbalances. In relationships marked by vulnerability, dependence and continued trust, the legally required rebalancing cannot be limited to the economic account, because contractual injury may also reach legitimate expectations, dignified treatment and the practical integrity of the consumption experience. It is in this direction that Marques warns that "focusing only on the economic imbalance of the consumer contract would be a limited view of the notion of contractual equity", since what is sought is "the total rebalancing of the relationship, including its level of loyal and dignified treatment", the only way to maintain and protect the legitimate expectations of the parties <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 290)</2>. This broadening is decisive if the existential item is to remain anchored in the dogmatic ground of consumer law. In the same vein, the author observes that the principle of trust leads the CDC system to protect the adequacy, quality and reasonable safety of products and services, its ultimate purpose being "to improve the quality of life of Brazilians" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1481)</4>. Consumer protection thus also reaches injuries that go beyond narrow economic loss. <5>↩</5>

The protection of trust and the application of objective good faith also bear on the design of the available legal remedies themselves, ruling out the idea that every relevant contractual injury must be converted solely into patrimonial compensation. When the consumer relationship frustrates legitimate expectations as to the adequacy, utility, safety or quality of the performance, the consumer-law system seeks, first and foremost, to restore the consumer's position materially. Marques, in dealing with the legal guarantee of adequacy, stresses that it aims to "satisfy the interests" of the consumer, whether by "perfect performance of the obligation", by "rebalancing between the performances rendered", or by avoiding greater harm and compensating that already suffered, grounding this guarantee in the trust legitimately aroused and in the mandatory good faith of the supplier in the market <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1383)</2>. The author reinforces this reading by arguing that, without an effective legal reaction to the frustration of trust and to the breach of ancillary duties, such commands would become "words in the wind", which is why the law of damages in the CDC fulfills not only a compensatory function, but also a preventive and satisfactory one, reaching even non-patrimonial damages and negative interests <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 856)</4>. This supports the opening of the system to remedies of restoration that are functionally richer than the mere monetization of the loss. <5>↩</5>

By way of complementary methodological deepening, it is worth noting that Brazilian law has already seen moves toward categorial refinement aimed at preventing injuries to the person from being absorbed, without analytical loss, by excessively broad and undifferentiated headings. Not every non-patrimonial injury can be adequately apprehended through the simple opposition between patrimonial damage and generic moral damages; there are cases in which the specificity of the affected legal interest requires denser conceptual treatment, precisely so that the protection of the person does not become too abstract <1>Lopez</1><2>(Lopez, 2021, p. 31-33)</2>. It is in this strict sense that the methodological parallel proves useful here. The individualization of aesthetic damage shows that civil liability can develop finer categories when it perceives that a certain dimension of personal injury has its own structure <3>Lopez</3><4>(Lopez, 2021, p. 78)</4>. The point of contact lies not in the material content of aesthetic damage, but in the dogmatic legitimacy of the operation of specification when the generality of the category no longer offers enough density to apprehend a given form of offense to the person. This parallel helps support the claim that injuries bearing on digital trajectory, history of enjoyment and biographical continuity may require denser analytical treatment than that offered by the undifferentiated heading of mere moral damages. <5>↩</5>

The sectoral regulation of electronic games matters, above all, because it dismantles two poor simplifications: the notion that the sector is legally invisible and the notion that naming it in legislation would suffice to resolve the central conflicts of its governance. The legal framework for electronic games expressly recognizes the existence of an industry of its own<1><2>582</2></1>, regulates its central economic chain — manufacture, import, commercialization, development and commercial use<3><4>583</4></3> — and provides a normative definition of what counts as an electronic game, including interactive audiovisual works developed as computer programs, devices and accessories, and software consumed by download or streaming<5><6>584</6></5>. The sector, therefore, can no <7>p. 544</7> longer be treated as a legally minor pastime or as a regulatory gray zone. The legislator named it, framed it and explicitly placed it within the horizon of legitimate economic activity, innovation and culture<8><9>585</9></8>.

This recognition, however, is framed in terms of regulated economic freedom. The law affirms the freedom of manufacture, import, commercialization, development and commercial use of electronic games, but does so with express reference to Article 173 of the Constitution and to the legislation in force<1><2>586</2></1>. This is relevant because the framework does not enshrine a sectoral free-for-all disguised as friendly modernity. On the contrary, it already reveals that the sector is conceived within a frame of legally conditioned economic freedom, including a specific public concern with age rating and with the risks related to the use of microtransaction mechanisms<3><4>587</4></3>. In other words, regulation does not operate as an external brake on the sector, but as a recognition that its economic activity mobilizes, at the same time, money, structural asymmetries and sensitive publics whose protection is part of the constitutional order itself.

The same logic appears in the substantive guidelines of the law itself. The framework organizes the sector institutionally through principles and guidelines<1><2>588</2></1> and, in the core most relevant to this thesis, affirms that electronic games must be conceived in light of respect for fundamental rights and democratic values, consumer protection, the integral protection of children and adolescents, and the preservation of privacy, the protection of personal data and <3>p. 545</3> informational self-determination<4><5>589</5></4>. The perspective is decisive because it shows that the legal order already treats the sector as an economic and cultural activity crossed by multisectoral public concerns, and not as a playful enclave left solely to private initiative. The dogmatic relevance of this lies in preventing any attempt at legal infantilization of the problem, as if electronic games still belonged to the regulatory limbo of “it's just entertainment”.

The Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents reinforces this diagnosis by making explicit, on another normative front, that the digital environment is not neutral and that suppliers are subject to positive duties of prevention, protection, information and safety<1><2>590</2></1>. The material content of the best interest of the child and adolescent, in this context, already encompasses privacy, safety, mental and physical health, access to information, freedom of participation in society and well-being<3><4>591</4></3>. The norm goes further than programmatic discourse by prohibiting <5>loot </5> <6>boxes</6> in games aimed at children and adolescents and banning profiling techniques for targeting commercial advertising<7><8>592</8></7>. With this, the legislator recognizes, head-on, that practices typical of the economic organization of electronic games may generate specific risks and warrant their own regulation. Sectoral normativity, therefore, already sees the games market as a site of sensitive monetization, behavioral formation and informational vulnerability.

The entry into force of the new protective regime made this perception even more concrete by directly reaching one of the most characteristic mechanisms of the contemporary monetization of electronic games. By prohibiting <1>loot boxes</1> in games aimed at children and adolescents, as well as in those likely to be accessed by this audience, the Digital Statute of Children and Adolescents not only abstractly recognized the economic and behavioral sensitivity of this market, but began to interfere in the very way products were organized that had previously been presented as fully compatible with the presence of minors in the digital ecosystem <2>Brasil</2><3>(Brasil, [2025]c)</3>. Bringing its entry into force forward to March 2026 reinforces <4>p. 546</4> this point because it shows that the legislator did not treat the matter as a merely symbolic or deferrable agenda item, but as a concrete regulatory problem, capable of requiring immediate adaptation by suppliers that structure their activity on mechanisms of microtransaction and recurrent capture of attention and spending <5>Brasil</5><6>(Brasil, [2026]b)</6>.

The institutional reaction of <1>Riot Games</1> to the new scenario shows, with particular sharpness, both the strength and the limit of sectoral regulation. Instead of immediately reorganizing the economic architecture of <2>League of Legends</2> to keep its offer compatible with the continued presence of underage users, the company chose to shift the response to the plane of access, announcing that minors could not play titles rated 18+ (for those over eighteen) in Brazil, not even with the consent of their guardians, and tying any restoration of enjoyment to the user's coming of age or to a future re-rating of the game<3><4>593</4></3> <5>Riot Games</5><6>(Riot Games, [2026]n)</6>. At the same time, the company itself clarified that any affected accounts would remain preserved, with items, cosmetics and progress maintained, although frozen until access was later released <7>Riot Games</7><8>(Riot Games, [2026]m)</8>. The fact is dogmatically telling because it reveals, in an almost confessional way, that the value of the consumer relationship is not exhausted by the isolated act of acquisition, nor can it be reduced to abstract ownership of digital records. What is in dispute is the continued enjoyment of a position built over time, whose utility depends on the user's remaining in the governed environment.

The episode offers an especially valuable demonstration, since sectoral regulation proves capable of recognizing specific risks and of pressuring the market, but the private response is still organized according to the logic proper to the <1>Lex Plataformae</1>, that is, through the unilateral reengineering of the conditions of access and permanence, and not through a spontaneous revision of the economic rationality that produced the problem. The result is revealing. Faced with the application of a public norm aimed at protecting children and adolescents, the platform preserves the monetization model and transfers to the vulnerable user the practical cost of adaptation, converting the former condition of tolerated and economically <2>p. 547</2> exploitable participant into a situation of temporary exclusion from the ecosystem. The methodological importance of this picture lies in showing, with rare clarity, that the sectoral framing of the games market is indispensable, but not sufficient. It sees the risk, names the sector and produces relevant commands; it does not, by itself, solve the dogmatic problem of continuous enjoyment subjected to opaque, mutable and unilaterally administered private governance.

Nor should it be perceived as a kind of loose regulation, devoid of sanction. The statute imposes concrete duties to remove content that violates rights and requires a legal representative in the country with powers to receive service of process<1><2>594</2></1>, while the regulating decree designates an administrative authority, provides for blocking orders and even activates the technical infrastructural layer of the digital environment through coordination with Anatel and CGI.br<3><4>595</4></3>. This is important because it dismantles the presentation of the platform as a self-sufficient sovereign space. The digital environment is already an object of public institutionality, with authorities, orders, enforcement mechanisms and mandatory points of contact. Pure self-regulation, in this scenario, poorly describes the state of the law in force.

At the same time, the normative recognition of the sector also has repercussions on the structural regime of industrial property. The amendment made by the legal framework in inserting the grant of registration for electronic games into the Industrial Property Law<1><2>596</2></1> shows that games came to be regarded, more robustly, as an object of legal protection within the innovation economy. This matters for the thesis because it confirms that the sector was assimilated by the legal order not only as a cultural and market activity, but also as a reality capable of radiating consequences into the regimes of exclusivity. The consequence, however, is not to turn intellectual property into the total language of the problem. On the contrary, it makes it all the more necessary to contain the proprietarist temptation to capture entirely conflicts that, on the plane of enjoyment, remain conflicts of governed consumption.

This whole sectoral repertoire is relevant for describing the sector, recognizing its institutional categories, identifying typical forms of monetization and making explicit specific public <1>p. 548</1> concerns. But it does not, by itself, deliver the dogmatic solution to the central problem of the IOC. What is at stake is not only the institutional recognition of the industry, nor the affirmation that electronic games are innovation, culture or regulated economic activity. The decisive point lies in the structure of private power that shapes the continuous enjoyment of the consumed immaterial object. And this structure is not resolved by the mere fact that the sector has its own legal framework.

The central conflict remains elsewhere: in continued performance, in architectural opacity, in unilateral control of access, in relevant changes of enjoyment, in the modulation of visibility, in the administration of inventories, histories and reputations, in evidentiary asymmetry and in the private distribution of the conditions of permanence in the ecosystem. None of this disappears because the sector received a name and principles in law. Sectoral framing helps us see the market; it is not enough to control governance. In IOCs, immaterial product and governed environment are dogmatically inseparable, and for this reason the application of norms cannot be exhausted by the economic-cultural framing of the sector. It must reach the administered enjoyment and the <1>Lex Plataformae</1> that organizes it.

This insufficiency does not disqualify sectoral regulation. It only repositions its reach. The games framework, the protective digital statute and the complementary normativity function as an important repertoire of recognition, public signaling of risks and institutional delimitation of the sector. They show what the State has already perceived: that electronic games mobilize innovation, culture, data, consumption, childhood, advertising, microtransactions and economic power. But the dogmatic problem of the IOC requires an additional step. It requires articulating this repertoire with the constitutional economic order, with the CDC and, in tension, with intellectual property, to face what sectoral regulation does not solve alone: continuous enjoyment as a consumer relationship subjected to opaque and mutable private governance.

The existence of sectoral regulation does not replace the consumer-law infrastructure, nor does it authorize conflicts of enjoyment to be fully absorbed by the grammar of the sector or by the language of innovation. The sector may be recognized, promoted and legally named, and still the decisive question may remain open: what limits apply when the platform unilaterally reconfigures access, use, visibility, continuity and functional equivalence of the consumed immaterial object?

It is this question that the sectoral repertoire, on its own, does not answer. And it is precisely for this reason that the protection of the IOC must be built not on a fetish for the “games framework”, but on the articulation between sectoral regulation, consumer protection, the constitutional economic order and limits on the private exercise of platform powers.

In Brazilian law, consumer protection does not occupy a peripheral position, nor can it be reduced to a corrective technique for episodic contractual imbalances. It forms part of the very rationality of the constitutional and economic order, insofar as it expresses a structural commitment to containing asymmetries, limiting private powers and preserving the material conditions of liberty and dignity in market relations. In platform environments, this takes on special relevance, because economic activity no longer presents itself merely as an offer of utilities and comes to involve the continuous administration of the conditions of access to, permanence in, intelligibility, visibility and challenge of enjoyment. Private power, in this context, no longer operates only through setting prices or drafting clauses, but through the coordination of architecture, curation, sanction and the ordinary management of the consumption environment.

This mutation does not require a rupture with the legal order in force, but a more demanding reading of its own premises. Consumer protection as a fundamental right and principle of the economic order already offers sufficient basis to frame, without artificiality, private forms of government that produce broad and repeated effects on the experience of enjoyment, even if they are not to be confused with state power. When the platform concentrates faculties of modulating access, reorganizing visibility, altering the conditions of use, filtering evidence and practically defining the channels of challenge, the problem ceases to be only that of supplying a good or service in a static sense and becomes that of the institutionalized exercise of private economic power over positions of continued enjoyment. The constitutional reading of the market, therefore, does not serve here as a decorative frame, but as a criterion of intelligibility and limitation.

<1>p. 503</1> It is on this plane that it becomes necessary to name the Lex Plataformae. The expression designates the private ordering through which the platform structures and governs the enjoyment of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, articulating terms of use, community standards, interfaces, hierarchies of visibility, enforcement systems, update routines, evidence regimes and customer service practices into a unitary practical normativity. It is not a metaphor to ornament the digital, but an analytical category aimed at making legally visible what would otherwise appear fragmented among contract, technique and everyday operation. Its core lies not in an isolated instrument nor in a specific algorithm, but in the institutional coordination of heterogeneous mechanisms that produce consistent normative effects on who accesses, how one remains, what can be perceived, what can be lost and on what terms the loss can be understood or challenged.

The platform thus ceases to be read as a neutral support or a mere channel of intermediation and comes to be recognized as a private center that organizes the consumption experience. In ecosystems of continued enjoyment, value is not exhausted at the initial delivery, because it depends on the persistence of technical, symbolic and organizational conditions that remain under the supplier's control. The utility consumed is realized over time, under permanent updating and curation, so that the consumer's vulnerability stems not only from a lack of information about the object's characteristics, but also from structural dependence on the signs, metrics, interfaces and framings through which this object becomes intelligible, comparable and verifiable. It is precisely this administered dependence that explains why, on platforms, the asymmetry is not only informational or economic in the classical sense, but also semiotic.

The Constitution, the Consumer Protection Code and the intellectual property regimes do not apply here as watertight blocks competing for abstract primacy, but as sources simultaneously summoned by one and the same legal problem. Their coordination must follow a systematic logic compatible with the openness of the consumer-law microsystem and with the need to prevent both its isolation and its capture by a purely contractual or proprietary grammar. It is not a matter of adding norms at random, but of recognizing that the governed enjoyment of the IOC simultaneously triggers constitutional requirements limiting economic power, consumer-law duties protecting vulnerability and functional limits on the exercise of private positions founded on exclusivity and technical control.

On this basis, the analysis that follows starts from the constitutional framing of consumer protection as a technique for containing private power with relevant public <1>p. 504</1> effects and moves on to reconstruct the criteria by which this power becomes institutionalized in platform environments. The aim is neither to moralize business choices nor to dissolve the technical specificity of these ecosystems into generic formulas of abuse. What is sought, rather, is to produce decidable categories, capable of bringing back into controllable legal language what, in the ordinary functioning of platforms, usually appears as mere technical necessity, a rule of the system or an inevitable consequence of infrastructure. Without this movement, the opacity of design remains naturalized and the consumer's governed experience continues to escape the traditional forms of attribution and control.
