The product-service dichotomy reappears here not as a metaphysical enigma to be solved with a scholastic ruler, but as an instrumental variable for calibrating specific legal consequences in supplies that extend over time. With IOCs, enjoyment is not exhausted at the moment of initial availability, because it depends on continued maintenance, updating, modulation and administration by the supplier. As a result, the distinction between <1>p. 558</1> immaterial good and performance activity remains legally useful, but insufficient as the sole axis for grasping the conflict. What is protected is not a frozen snapshot of the bond, but a consumption experience whose utility is realized and measured throughout performance. The legal structure remains in place: the CDC distinguishes product, including immaterial product, and service as an activity supplied in the market<2><3>610</3></2>, but this distinction only fulfills its function when read in light of the actual mode of enjoyment of the object consumed.

Therefore, the continuous supply of IOCs strains the classical model built around a completable delivery. The traditional logic works best when there is a relatively clear point of delivery and when inadequacy can be perceived by contrasting what was received with what should have been delivered. In lasting digital bonds, this point becomes blurred. The promised utility is not fulfilled all at once, because it remains dependent on the ecosystem that sustains it. Initial access may well occur without a hitch, but enjoyment may be downgraded later, through successive mutations, functional suppressions, silent reconfigurations or changes of environment that preserve the formal shell of the performance while corroding its concrete utility. Hence the importance of Article 26 of the CDC<1><2>611</2></1>, since it evidences the tension between the classical periods for ascertaining a quality defect and continuous performances in which inadequacy may emerge progressively, requiring a rereading of the point of cognizability instead of rigid fixation on the date of first access<3><4>612</4></3>.

The decisive technical point lies in placing quality defect and inadequacy back at the center of the analysis. In the CDC, the logic of quality of performance depends neither on dramatic collapse nor on <1>p. 559</1> absolute uselessness. It operates on the basis of the concrete aptitude of the product or service to achieve the purpose legitimately expected by the consumer. For the IOC, this means that protection does not depend on proving the “disappearance” of the object; it is sufficient to show that enjoyment ceased to correspond, in a legally relevant way, to the functional standard that was part of the relationship. A product or service presents a quality defect of adequacy when it no longer corresponds to the legitimate expectation of use or enjoyment, or when the nonconformity compromises its serviceability<2><3>613</3></2>. In continuous bonds, therefore, relevant inadequacy is measured less by ostensive rupture and more by the maintenance, over time, of the utility legitimately incorporated into the bond<4><5>614</5></4>.

This is the point at which the parallel with long-term captive contracts becomes methodologically fertile. Not because the IOC should be forced into this category as if it solved everything, but because it helps to visualize something that continuous digital consumption lays bare: performance is not exhausted at the initial adhesion, and the bond comes to be structured by practical dependence, permanent asymmetry, sedimented trust and the supplier's renewed power of imposition over time. Lasting relationships, organized through mass contracting and an architecture opaque to the consumer, create captivity and dependence, <1>p. 560</1> intensifying duties of information, cooperation, loyalty and protection of trust<2><3>615</3></2>. The consumer user of an IOC does not merely consume access, but enters a relationship marked by a legitimate expectation of continued access in an environment in which the future enjoyment of what they acquire remains subordinated to the private organization of the ecosystem.

It follows that contractual performance, in this type of bond, cannot be read as a simple sum of isolated performances. The obligation takes on a dynamic shape, projected in successive phases, and comes to incorporate legitimate expectations of stability, continuity and predictability. The contract ceases to be a one-off event and reveals itself as a program of performance developed over time, requiring collaboration, loyalty and respect for the concrete way in which enjoyment was organized and legitimately entrusted by the consumer<1><2>616</2></1>. The investment of trust arises not only from the initial promise, but also from repeated practice, from the continuity of utility and from the predictability of conduct that the supplier progressively sediments. Where this trust is built, unilateral changes or excessive instabilities affect not only the main performance, but the very contractual program concretely lived<3><4>617</4></3>.

Lasting bonds attract the ancillary duties of conduct with special intensity. Good faith, probity, qualified information, cooperation and protection of trust cease to be <1>p. 561</1> moral adornments of performance and become part of the very structure of supply<2><3>618</3></2>. Long-term relationships carry expectations that do not fit the instantaneous model of exchange, because they rest on repeated coexistence, maintenance of service quality and a capacity to adapt without betraying the contracted utility<4><5>619</5></4>. With IOCs, this means that the protected core of the relationship is exhausted neither by the initial consent nor by the literal reading of the pre-drafted clauses; it includes the trust legitimately built around the material continuity of enjoyment.

This frame also reinforces the limit on unilateral mutability. The continued contract is not a space of the supplier's private sovereignty merely because performance remains open over time. Contractual freedom finds limits in the social function of the contract<1><2>620</2></1>, and, in continued consumer relationships, this limitation takes on a very concrete form: the power to alter, modulate or reconfigure performance cannot be exercised so as to frustrate the function that justified the consumer's original acquisition. In captive contracts, clauses that concentrate excessive discretionary power of revision in the supplier may place it in a position incompatible with good faith and with the stability of the promises that gave meaning to the adhesion<3><4>621</4></3>.

On the more classical plane of the CDC, this prohibition already appears with sufficient clarity. A clause authorizing unilateral modification of the content or quality of the performance after contracting is null, because it turns the consumer into a compulsory recipient <1>p. 562</1> of a utility inferior to the one they legitimately acquired<2><3>622</3></2>. With IOCs, this rule gains surgical importance. The lowering need not come disguised as total cancellation; it may appear as a functional <4>downgrade</4>, compression of resources, loss of relational utility or systematic instability of the environment. Even so, it remains legally relevant because it breaks the balance of the relationship and diminishes the functional value of enjoyment without compatible restoration. Article 18 of the CDC<5><6>623</6></5> therefore remains the central door for framing a relevant quality defect in a continuous environment, now measured by the yardstick of functional equivalence and not only by the classical image of the spoiled product on the shelf.

Nor does the offer disappear after adhesion. In lasting relationships, information, advertising and contractual performance remain connected, so that the promised content continues to function as a parameter of the performance's adequacy. All sufficiently precise information becomes part of the contract and binds the supplier<1><2>624</2></1>, and this holds with special force when the utility consumed is mediated by interface, visual presentation, promises of progression and the digital externalization of the experience. In the CDC, clear and adequate information does not govern only the pre-contractual moment; it affects the essence of the deal throughout the relationship, and a failure in it may constitute a quality defect of the performance<3><4>625</4></3>. In the digital environment, this is especially important because the “shop window” is not merely advertising: it is part of the very <5>p. 563</5> substance of the IOC acquired. What was shown, described, promised and reiterated to the consumer continues to serve as a yardstick against opportunistic downgrades<6><7>626</7></6>.

The remedial consequence follows this logic. In lasting relationships, the relevant inadequacy of the performance need not be forced into the narrower filters of classical civil law, as if every revision depended on heroic unpredictability or contractual catastrophe. On the consumer-law plane, the breakdown of the objective basis of the deal, of the intrinsic balance of performances or of the essential purpose of the bond is enough to open room for revisional, resolutory or restorative protection<1><2>627</2></1>. In contracts of duration, this means that the relevant frustration of the utility legitimately incorporated into the relationship is already sufficient to trigger the protective system. The consumer may demand maintenance of the bond with correction of the performance, modification of the harmful clause, functional restoration of the utility or, as a last resort, rescission with the appropriate effects. Continuous performance does not reduce protection; it only changes the way of measuring the harm and choosing the remedy.

<1>p. 564</1> This technical point is decisive because, in IOCs, performance projects itself into the future as a succession of periodic performances and counter-performances, but also as a legitimate expectation of maintenance of enjoyment over time. Where continuity is part of the contracted utility itself, quality defects, periods and remedies cannot be read as if everything had ended at the initial availability<2><3>628</3></2>. The relationship is not exhausted at the first activation, the first download or the first login. What is also protected is the material preservation of the enjoyment legitimately expected in the course of the bond. This changes the reading of inadequacy, of ascertainment and of legal response.

For this reason, the product-service dichotomy must be kept under strict methodological discipline. It matters insofar as it allows specific normative consequences to be adjusted, such as the technical regime of quality defects, the point of ascertainment, the applicable remedies and the calibration between functional restoration and compensation. It does not matter as a totalizing ontological key to the IOC. The utility consumed in a continuous digital environment is often hybrid: it involves an immaterial good and an activity of maintenance, access and modulation, without this authorizing the dispersal of protection into classificatory preciosity<1><2>629</2></1>. The central problem lies elsewhere: performance exists only as governed enjoyment, and it is this governance that must be made controllable by law.

Thus, product and service are not obstacles to the regime of the IOC; they are instruments for adjusting specific effects in a consumption whose utility depends on the ecosystem that maintains, alters and administers it. The classificatory debate matters only insofar as it helps to stabilize legitimate expectations, control relevant unilateral reconfigurations and structure remedies compatible with the continuity of performance. Everything else is conceptual filigree with little power to solve the real problem. And the real problem, here, is the private administration of enjoyment.

The distinction between product and service, in the CDC, has real dogmatic utility, but it functions as a tool for organizing the protective regime, not as an ontological prison intended to narrow the Code's incidence. Article 3, paragraph 1, anchors the product on the plane of goods, encompassing a movable or immovable, material or immaterial object, while paragraph 2 brings the service back to the plane of activity supplied in the market for remuneration <1>Filomeno</1><2>(Filomeno, 2011, p. 51-53)</2>. In continuous and complex relationships, good and activity frequently appear functionally intertwined, without this authorizing the dissolution of consumer-law protection into classificatory preciosity. The legally relevant point remains the economically supplied utility and the way it is delivered, maintained or degraded in the course of the relationship. <3>↩</3>

“Art. 26. The right to complain about apparent or easily ascertainable quality defects lapses in: I - thirty days, in the case of supply of services and non-durable products; II - ninety days, in the case of supply of services and durable products. Paragraph 1. The lapse period begins to run from the effective delivery of the product or the end of the performance of the services. Paragraph 2. The following prevent the lapse: I - the complaint demonstrably made by the consumer to the supplier of products and services until the corresponding negative response, which must be transmitted unequivocally; [...] III - the institution of a civil inquiry, until its conclusion. Paragraph 3. In the case of a hidden quality defect, the lapse period begins at the moment the defect becomes evident.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. <3>↩</3>

The discipline of Article 26 of the CDC must be read in a key compatible with performances whose inadequacy is not revealed all at once. For apparent quality defects, the lapse period runs from the effective delivery of the product or the end of the performance of the service; for hidden quality defects, however, the starting point shifts to the moment the defect becomes evident <1>Denari</1><2>(Denari, 2011, p. 244)</2>. In continued relationships, the period cannot be used to turn the initial formal delivery into an artificial point for the early emptying of consumer-law protection. The count must engage with the real moment at which the inadequacy becomes cognizable, above all when it only emerges in prolonged use or in the supervening deterioration of serviceability <3>Denari</3><4>(Denari, 2011, p. 243-245)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Product, service, quality defect and inadequacy make up, in the CDC, a single systematic logic of control of the quality of performance, which makes it possible to frame lasting supply relationships without depending only on more sophisticated constructions about long-term captive contracts. The theory of quality explains that quality defects branch into two categories, the second being precisely that of “quality defects by inadequacy”, linked to the performance of products and services and to the fulfillment of their purpose in conformity with the legitimate expectation of the consumer <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 252])</2>. This structure projects itself directly onto Articles 18, 20 and 26 of the CDC. While liability for product-caused accidents deals primarily with safety, liability for quality defects has as its main focus the “real adequacy to the proper purposes” of the product or service, that is, its concrete aptitude to achieve the legitimately expected utility <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 318])</4>. The Manual itself summarizes the idea by observing that a product or service will present a quality defect of adequacy whenever it does not correspond to the legitimate expectation of the consumer as to its use or enjoyment, or when the nonconformity compromises its serviceability <5>Bessa</5><6>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 121])</6>. In this sense, the discipline of quality defects in the CDC is organized less by the abstract ontology of the object and more by the material idea of adequacy of performance. A product or service will be legally defective when it does not correspond to the legitimate expectation of the consumer as to its use or enjoyment, that is, when the nonconformity compromises its serviceability or usability <7>Denari</7><8>(Denari, 2011, p. 191)</8>. There is a quality defect when the performance proves inadequate for the purposes reasonably expected of it or when it does not meet the regulatory standards of serviceability <9>Denari</9><10>(Denari, 2011, p. 230)</10>. In continuous supplies, this means that the nominal survival of the bond is not enough; the protection of the CDC requires effective maintenance of the functional aptitude that legitimately became part of the relationship. <11>↩</11>

On the technical plane, the consumer-law protection of continued bonds is organized around the notion of quality defect as a failure of the duty of adequacy, and not only of defect in the sense of a risk to safety. A quality defect arises when a product or service does not serve the purpose legitimately expected of it, owing to the impairment of its quality or quantity <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 487])</2>. In continuous relationships of enjoyment, this shifts the focus from the extraordinary collapse of performance to the ordinary frustration of its utility. The quality defect of the product or service stems from the absence of properties or characteristics necessary to meet the purposes legitimately expected by the consumer, and amounts to the frustration of the presumable and reasonably expected utility of the product or service <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 523])</4>. In continuous supplies of IOCs, inadequacy must be measured by the maintenance, over time, of the utility legitimately expected by the consumer. <5>↩</5>

The category of long-term captive contracts offers an especially fertile dogmatic basis for understanding the continuous supply of IOCs as a complex, lasting and structurally asymmetric legal relationship. The bond is not exhausted in an instantaneous exchange, nor is it reduced to a snapshot of the initial moment of adhesion. It is a continued relationship, sustained by mass contracting methods, by a business organization opaque to the consumer and by a logic of permanence that turns enjoyment into practical dependence. This is precisely the movement captured in the description of "new contracts or contractual relationships" that, through adhesion contracts and general conditions, supply special services and create "complex long-term legal relationships", marked by the "position of 'captivity' or 'dependence' of the clients, consumers" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 77-78)</2>. Keeping the bond alive may lead the consumer to readily accept any new imposition by the supplier, guaranteeing the latter a constantly renewed "power of imposition" throughout the long-term obligation <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 109-110)</4>. It is this grammar of captivity that justifies the intensification, in such relationships, of the duties of information, cooperation, loyalty and protection of trust. <5>↩</5>

Understanding lasting bonds requires abandoning the static reading of the contract as an event concentrated in a single moment of formation. The obligation must be read as a dynamic bond developed in successive phases, capable of radiating duties of protection and cooperation beyond the performance of the main obligation <1>Martins-Costa</1><2>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 232-233)</2>. The parties bind themselves around a true “program of performance”, to which they are bound by virtue of self-binding and whose implementation requires intersubjective collaboration <3>Martins-Costa</3><4>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 236)</4>. Objective good faith requires respect for the concrete way in which enjoyment was organized, maintained and legitimately entrusted by the consumer over time. Unilateral changes or excessive instability affect the very contractual program as actually lived and the trust that has settled within it. <5>↩</5>

In continued contractual relationships, performance is not exhausted at the initial delivery, because the bond also comes to be structured by expectations of stability, predictability and loyalty formed in the course of the relationship. When enjoyment is prolonged, the contractual program also comprises the concrete pattern of performance settled between the parties. The duties to act in good faith must be assessed in connection with the investment of trust legitimized by the predictability of conduct, so that the duties of loyalty lie at the point where the legitimate expectations of those who trust cannot be disloyally undermined <1>Martins-Costa</1><2>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 309)</2>. In the continuous supply of IOCs, repeated practice and trust settled over time become part of the legally relevant bond. <3>↩</3>

“Art. 422. The contracting parties are obliged to observe, both in the conclusion of the contract and in its performance, the principles of probity and good faith.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]a)</2>. <3>↩</3>

Lasting contractual relationships attract, with special intensity, the incidence of ancillary duties of conduct, because the bond ceases to be understood as a one-off act of exchange and comes to be read as a continued process of legally relevant interaction. Within this framework, the obligation is no longer limited to the main performance, but projects itself over time as a complex of behaviors, expectations and reciprocal responsibilities. It is "a new view of the obligation, as a complex of acts, conducts, duties extending over time", objective good faith being a source of duties "to inform, to cooperate, duty of care, of secrecy, of advice, of loyalty etc." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 110-111)</2>. The long-term contract "carries within it expectations other than those of contracts of immediate performance", since it is based "more on trust, on repeated coexistence, on the maintenance of economic potential and of the quality of services", which is why "the capacity for adaptation, for cooperation between contracting parties, for continuation of the contractual relationship is basic" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1222)</4>. This supports reading the continuous supply of IOCs as a performance whose protected core is not exhausted in the initial consent. <5>↩</5>
“Art. 421. Contractual freedom shall be exercised within the limits of the social function of the contract.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]a)</2>. <3>↩</3>

In continued bonds, the control of supervening changes cannot be thought of only in formal terms of renewed consent or of the abstract possibility of renegotiation. The duration of the relationship intensifies dependence, trust and the practical centrality of the performance, requiring that the stability of the contractual program function as a parameter for containing the supplier's modifying power. Clauses imposed in relationships aimed precisely at future security and at the "maintenance of the contractually agreed promises and conditions" may represent "an excessive [...] discretionary power, placing the consumer at an excessive disadvantage contrary to good faith", allowing a factually "unilateral" variation of the content of the contract, of the performances and of the price <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1225)</2>. In relational and captive contracts, revisions and readaptations cannot "authorize abuses of the dominant contractual position" nor frustrate legitimate expectations of the parties, and must operate according to cooperation, loyalty and good faith <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 101)</4>. <5>↩</5>

The prohibition on unilateral downgrading of the utility delivered to the consumer finds direct dogmatic formulation in Article 51, item XIII, of the CDC. A clause that purports to authorize the supplier to alter, by its exclusive will, the content or quality of the performance after contracting is null, since this breaks the balance of the relationship and turns the consumer into a compulsory recipient of a utility inferior to that which he legitimately acquired. Commenting on the provision, Nunes notes the nullity of the clause that authorizes “the supplier to unilaterally modify the content or quality of the contract, after its conclusion”, illustrating the abuse with a case in which the supplier reduces, without reducing the price, the intensity of the agreed performance <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 508-509])</2>. The quality defect constitutes “a minus of the consumer's right” and admitting a quantitatively or qualitatively inferior performance would amount to tolerating “the unlawful enrichment and unjust enrichment of the supplier” <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 184])</4>. <5>↩</5>

“Art. 18. Suppliers of durable or non-durable consumer products are jointly and severally liable for quality or quantity defects that render them unfit or inadequate for the consumption for which they are intended or that diminish their value […].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. <3>↩</3>

“Art. 30. All sufficiently precise information or advertising, conveyed by any form or means of communication with respect to products and services offered or presented, binds the supplier that conveys it or makes use of it and becomes part of the contract that may be concluded.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. <3>↩</3>

Offer, information and contractual performance remain legally connected throughout the consumer relationship, so that the promised or presented content continues to function as a parameter of adequacy of the performance during the execution of the bond. The Manual points out that the requirement of clear and adequate information is not limited to the pre-contractual moment, but also governs the conclusion of the contract, the contract itself and the post-contractual moment; for this reason, information “affects the essence of the deal”, becoming part of the contractual content and, if it fails, possibly constituting a quality defect in the product or service offered <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 126])</2>. The binding effect is reinforced when the work explains that it acts in two ways: first, obliging the supplier even if it refuses to contract; second, entering into and prevailing in any contract that may be concluded, even when the contractual text itself tries to remove this binding character <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 404])</4>. In addition, Article 48 of the CDC is read in the Manual as a command according to which declarations of will contained in private writings, receipts and pre-contracts bind the supplier, and may even give rise to specific performance, so that “everything that is said and offered” in the name of the supplier already produces legal effects and constitutes a contractual clause <5>Bessa</5><6>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 597])</6>. <7>↩</7>

In the CDC regime, the offer does not operate as a simple preparatory phase or neutral invitation to contract, but as a legally binding element of the consumer relationship itself. The consumer-law discipline breaks with the narrow privatist logic and recognizes that the offering message already produces an obligation for the supplier, which is bound to the content externalized to the market. “Every offer relating to products and services binds the offering supplier, obliging it to fulfill what it offers” <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 310])</2>. This binding effect also covers the presentation of the product or service, including visual display as a legally relevant fact: “the mere presentation of the product in the shop window, on the shelf, on the counter etc.” also constitutes an offer, the conveyed message being “the evidentiary element of its existence and binding effect” <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 312])</4>. This is especially useful for consumption environments mediated by interface, in which the visual externalization of utility is part of the offered content itself. <5>↩</5>

Quality defect, breach of the offer and alteration of the content of the performance may trigger, in the CDC, remedies of material restoration, and not only formal or pecuniary solutions. Declarations of will contained in private writings, receipts and pre-contracts bind the supplier and their breach may give rise to specific performance under Article 84, precisely to achieve the “practical result equivalent to that of performance” of the obligation <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 597])</2>. Faced with a nonconforming offer, the consumer may demand forced performance of the obligation, accept another equivalent consumer good or rescind the contract with restitution of what he paid and losses and damages <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 408])</4>. In case of a quality defect, the CDC allows the consumer to demand another product of the same kind in perfect conditions of use, alongside restitution or proportional price reduction <5>Bessa</5><6>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 338])</6>. The consumer-law system, therefore, is not content with the nominal survival of the performance when the promised utility was downgraded or diverted. In lasting relationships, the relevant inadequacy of the performance triggers consumer-law remedies of their own, without submission to the narrower filters of classical civil law. Article 6 of the CDC advances in relation to the Civil Code's regime of excessive onerousness precisely by not requiring unpredictability or irresistibility of the supervening fact, the breakdown of the objective basis of the deal, of the intrinsic balance between performances or the disappearance of the essential purpose of the contract being sufficient <7>Bessa</7><8>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 133])</8>. The consequence is decisive for continued contracts: the relevant frustration of the utility legitimately incorporated into the bond is already sufficient to open room for revisional or resolutory protection of the consumer. This logic appears even more concretely in Article 20 of the CDC. Faced with quality defects that diminish the value of the service, the consumer may demand contractual rescission without penalty or proportional price reduction, with no need to discuss the supplier's fault, since it is strict liability <9>Bessa</9><10>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 354])</10>. In contracts of duration, it is well known that one may request either the modification of the clause with maintenance of the bond or the rescission of the contract, with a declaration of nullity of the abusive clause or its modification if excessively onerous <11>Bessa</11><12>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 136-137])</12>. <13>↩</13>

In contracts of continued performance, periodic performances are not exhausted in their simple one-off realization, because they project into the future the satisfaction of the legitimate interests of the consumer. In these relationships, the structure of the bond becomes that of successive periodic performances and counter-performances, also encompassing the legitimate expectation of their maintenance over time <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 393])</2>. The need to preserve the legitimate expectations of continuity of the contract may imply constant readaptation of the contractual relationship, precisely to avoid its frustration <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 393])</4>. In continuous supplies of IOCs, performance is not exhausted at the first availability of access or functionality; what is also protected is the material continuity of the enjoyment legitimately expected in the course of the bond. Where performance projects itself into the future, quality defects, periods and remedies cannot be read as if everything had ended at the first click. <5>↩</5>

In a dogmatic key, the elementary distinction between product and service must be stabilized without losing sight of the protective functionality of the CDC. The service is identified, at its core, with the idea of activity, that is, with purposively oriented human action, whose realization is consumed in its very exercise. While the product falls under the category of good, the service falls under the category of doing: “service is, typically, activity”, this being “human action that has a purpose in view”, so that “every action is exhausted as soon as it is performed” <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 102])</2>. This differentiation, however, does not prevent the recognition of mixed situations, in which the activity performed makes use of goods that accompany or enable it. There are services “rendered with products that make up the service itself” and that, even so, “continue to be characterized as a service” <3>Nunes</3><4>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 113])</4>. <5>↩</5>

The starting point of the regime of the IOC does not lie in resolving, with taxonomic solemnity, whether continuous digital supply would be “more product” or “more service”. The distinction exists in the system, has real dogmatic utility and will remain relevant for specific purposes of <1>p. 551</1> periods, quality defects, remedies and calibration of consequences<2><3>597</3></2>. The error lies in turning it into an ontological prison. In governed digital ecosystems, consumption is no longer organized according to the paradigm of the one-off delivery of a stable utility, but according to the paradigm of the continuous maintenance, updating and modulation of enjoyment under private control. Within this framework, product and service remain operative, but cease to function as the exclusive key of intelligibility of the conflict. The center of the problem becomes the relationship of administered enjoyment.

This derives from the very way the CDC was built. The final recipient remains the subjective point of reference of the system<1><2>598</2></1>, and the supplier remains identified by its professional insertion in the consumer market. But the legal concepts of product and service were formulated in a deliberately open way, precisely to prevent narrow readings that leave out immaterial supplies, hybrid arrangements and complex structures of performance. A product is any good, including immaterial, and a service is any activity supplied in the market for remuneration, which reveals from the outset that the system was not designed to protect only corporeal things and simple performances <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 194; p. 193; p. 272])</4><5><6>599</6></5>. Therefore, it is not a matter of forcing an extension of the legal text; it is only a matter of reading it free of any conceptual claustrophobia.

This is also why the distinction between product and service cannot be conducted as an exercise in dogmatic taxidermy. In consumer matters, the utility of categories depends on their capacity to solve the protective problem, and not on satisfying a classificatory purism indifferent to the way supply really operates. Consumer law works with more open and functional concepts because they only acquire meaning <1>p. 552</1> in light of the problem to be solved, and it is this key that prevents using the product-service dichotomy as an exclusionary filter of protection in continuous and governed digital supplies <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 219-220; p. 149-150)</3><4><5>600</5></4>. The point is not to abolish the distinction, but to refuse its fetishization.

This reading becomes even clearer when one observes that the CDC itself starts from relational categories and not from isolated essences. Consumer, supplier, product and service only make dogmatic sense within a concrete supply relationship, and not as watertight compartments capable of deciding everything alone. The system was designed to capture the economic dynamics actually in place, not to reward whoever best plays at classifying the world into elegant little boxes <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 31; p. 139])</2><3><4>601</4></3>. In <5>p. 553</5> complex digital supplies, this is decisive: the central question is not whether the object fits comfortably into a civilist ontology inherited from another technological environment, but whether there is a final recipient, a professional market agent and a utility supplied in a context of structural dependence.

It is in this respect that factual vulnerability manifests itself as the true interpretive infrastructure of the item. The CDC does not protect the consumer despite their fragility; it protects them because this fragility is the constitutive fact of the consumer relationship. Vulnerability is the starting point of the system and militates in favor of the final recipient precisely because the market is organized by asymmetries that the consumer does not control <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 168; p. 118; p. 166])</2><3><4>602</4></3>. In other words: the incidence of the CDC does not arise from the classificatory purity of the relationship, but from the presence of a vulnerable party before a supplier that unilaterally structures the conditions of supply.

This vulnerability, of course, is not limited to possible economic insufficiency. It is also technical, informational, organizational and practical. The consumer enters the market without taking part in the definition of the productive models, without controlling the processes that structure the offer and without mastering the criteria that organize the functioning of the good or service supplied. They receive models unilaterally designed by the supplier and are often not even in a position to fully understand their logic of operation <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 72; p. 457])</2><3><4>603</4></3>. In continuous digital environments, this asymmetry intensifies because supply <5>p. 554</5> does not end at the initial acquisition: it projects itself over time through infrastructure, updating, curation, restriction and continued intervention by the supplier in the user's experience.

The same holds for understanding the service and the consumed utility. Performance does not always present itself in a linear, simple and isolable form. There are composite services, utilities dependent on multiple agents, instrumental activities articulated with each other and performances whose enjoyment only exists because an entire technical, communicational and relational architecture keeps running in the background <1>Nunes</1><2>(Nunes, 2018, [p. 97; p. 198])</2><3><4>604</4></3>. This observation is particularly useful here because the IOC is not to be confused with a “digital file” nor with “momentary access”. Its enjoyment depends on an ecosystem that maintains, alters and administers it. For this reason legal control cannot remain stuck at the abstract instant of availability; it must reach the regime of maintenance of the acquired utility.

This was, moreover, already the material spirit of the CDC from its classical basis. The notion of service was conceived as any utility supplied in the market to the consumer, and the legislative choice for broad categories of goods and services pointed precisely to the real objects of interest of consumer relationships, and not to conceptual barriers intended to narrow protection <1>Filomeno</1><2>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 110])</2><3><4>605</4></3>. The system was born oriented to the utility concretely <5>p. 555</5> supplied to the final recipient, and not to terminological disputes disconnected from the protective function of the Code. This fact matters because it prevents regression to formalisms that the CDC itself had already overcome at the start.

Likewise, vulnerability was recognized early on as a structural presupposition of consumer-law protection, linked not only to the absence of bargaining power, but to the consumer's lack of control over products, services, information and functioning criteria defined by the supplier. In this field, then, the old dogmas of autonomy of the will in its pure version, of abstract equality and of contractual intangibility give way, since they presuppose a real parity that simply does not exist when the market is unilaterally organized by whoever supplies <1>Filomeno</1><2>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 61; p. 346])</2><3><4>606</4></3>. In a continuous digital environment, this perception ceases to be a theoretical detail and becomes the very key for reading the bond.

Contracting by adhesion, predisposed general conditions, network organization, practical dependence of the adhering party and difficulty in understanding the internal logic of the service are clear indications of factual vulnerability, even when the consumer has technical training or works professionally in another field. In long-term bonds, dependence may deepen to the point of frustrating relevant expectations if the relationship is interrupted or unilaterally reconfigured, which makes even less defensible a reading centered only <1>p. 556</1> on superficial classificatory labels <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 613; p. 109)</3><4><5>607</5></4>. This is why the IOC must be read from the standpoint of governed enjoyment, and not only from the formal appearance of an isolable performance.

In this context, factual vulnerability is not merely a backdrop; it is a criterion of interpretation. Consumer law belongs to the rights of protection precisely because it seeks to restore material equality in situations of real inequality, and this function is only achieved when the reading of the legal categories remains functional, broad and faithful to the structure of the market <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 34; p. 122])</2><3><4>608</4></3>. In other words, product, service, consumer and supplier only make sense within a system built to respond to <5>p. 557</5> vulnerability. When the analysis forgets this, it becomes high-level conceptual bureaucracy, but of low utility. A very refined specialty, but not very effective.

Offer, adequacy, information, trust, reparation and restoration must be read from the standpoint of governed enjoyment, and not only from the literal content of a detachable performance. The consumed object is inseparable from the ecosystem that sustains, modifies and administers it, which is why the center of control must shift to standards of controllability of the environment, verifiability of changes and minimum stability of the acquired experience. The product-service dichotomy remains relevant, but as an instrumental variable to calibrate specific consequences, not as a totem defining the entire regime.

In cases of unilateral downgrading of enjoyment, the door of the quality defect remains available<1><2>609</2></1>, precisely because relevant inadequacy need not take the crude form of total uselessness. It may appear as an objective decrease in the functional value of the enjoyment promised and maintained over time. In IOCs, this means that the discussion about quality defects cannot be captured by traditional images of a defect perceptible by direct inspection. Functional equivalence comes to operate as a ruler better suited to the problem: what matters is whether the acquired experience was degraded in a legally relevant way by the continuous regime of private governance.

The distinction between product and service exists, remains operative and will be dealt with more surgically further on. But, for the regime of the IOC, the true interpretive foundation lies in the factual vulnerability of the final recipient before an immaterial, continuous supply governed by a third party. It is this fact that authorizes rereading the CDC from the standpoint of administered enjoyment, and not of the old scene of the stable thing delivered once and for all.

Paragraph 1. A product is any good, movable or immovable, material or immaterial. Paragraph 2. A service is any activity supplied in the consumer market, for remuneration […].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. <3>↩</3>
“Art. 2. A consumer is any natural or legal person who acquires or uses a product or service as final recipient.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2022])</2>. <3>↩</3>

The concepts of product and service in the CDC were formulated in a deliberately open way, precisely to prevent a narrow reading that leaves out of consumer-law protection immaterial supplies, complex structures of performance and hybrid market arrangements. Paragraph 1 of Article 3 defines product as “any good, movable or immovable, material or immaterial”, which allows it to be understood beyond the narrower civil categories and to encompass goods consumable physically or not, new or used, fungible or non-fungible, principal or accessory <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 194])</2>. The same openness projects itself onto the concept of service. Paragraph 2 of Article 3 defines it as “any activity supplied in the consumer market, for remuneration”, with concise and intentionally open wording, precisely to ensure the inclusion of a wide number of providers and arrangements of performance within the field of incidence of the CDC <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 193])</4>. The Manual further stresses that the legislator did not build rigid concepts, but adopted a true “typological statement, flexible par excellence”, capable of reaching mixed acts, immaterial supplies and economically complex relationships <5>Bessa</5><6>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 272])</6>. <7>↩</7>

The reading of the categories of product and service within the CDC cannot be conducted as an exercise of rigid taxonomy, alien to the protective function of the microsystem. The distinction remains legally relevant, but must not operate as a classificatory jail capable of neutralizing the incidence of the consumer-law regime whenever supply takes technically hybrid, procedural or continuously governed forms, as happens with immaterial objects of consumption. In consumer matters, the dogmatic utility of categories depends on their capacity to solve the protective problem posed, and not on satisfying an ontological purism that, in the end, only serves to leave the consumer alone in the middle of the labyrinth. It is in this direction that Marques observes that consumer law moves away from the strict positivist ideal and adopts a problem-oriented style of thought, with concepts “more open, more functional, delimited without so much logical rigor”, precisely because they “only take on meaning in light of the problem to be solved” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 219-220)</2>. This functional key prevents the product-service distinction from being converted into an exclusionary filter of protection, above all when the bond involves continuous digital supplies, modulated over time by private architecture, updates, restrictions of use and unilateral reconfigurations. The point is not to abolish the categories, but to refuse their fetishized use against the purpose of the system. Marques argues precisely that the rules of the CDC must be interpreted according to the protective logic of the Code itself and in accordance with its normative purpose, which requires a teleological and not merely formal reading. In dealing with the definition of consumer, the author states that “the rule of art. 2 must be interpreted in accordance with the special protection system of the Code and in accordance with the purpose of the norm”, concluding that “only a teleological interpretation” allows the field of protection of the CDC to be adequately defined, including through openness to cases in which vulnerability proves legally relevant, even if certain traditional classificatory fits do not present themselves in their purest form <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 149-150)</4>. Applied to the present problem, this orientation authorizes privileging the protective function of the microsystem over excessive classificatory formalisms, so that the distinction between product and service continues to serve Law, and not the other way around. <5>↩</5>
